How causal mapping helps a real evaluation

The Love Alliance case

Steve and Gabriele at Causal Map, with Dena at Southern Hemisphere

The programme, and a flood of evidence

Part one

The programme, and a flood of evidence

The programme

A five-year partnership, 2021 to 2025, for the health and rights of key populations affected by HIV.

Sex workers, people who use drugs, LGBTQ+ people and people living with HIV, across ten African countries, plus regional and global advocacy.

Funded by the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs through Aidsfonds, delivered through advocacy, capacity-strengthening and movement building.

Southern Hemisphere ran the end-term evaluation. We supported them to bring causal mapping into it, with AI for scale.

The plan: a tidy ladder

The official theory of change: strategies at the bottom, then short, medium and long-term outcomes, then goals at the top. Clear, communicable, fundable. But a ladder cannot draw a loop.

The nicer problem: too much evidence

The usual complaint in evaluation is too little evidence. Here we had the opposite.

176

documents: 79 country reports, 97 transcripts

22,000

causal claims coded in total

13,756

factual links kept for the maps

AI as a clerk, not an oracle

A team hand-coding at that scale would be exhausted long before a defensible overview. Humans tire, get bored, pay uneven attention.

So the app uses the model as a low-level coding assistant. It finds and codes every claim across all 176 documents; the analysts write the instructions, check against the quotes, and decide what the map means.

The real question shifts: not how to squeeze a conclusion from too little, but how to keep faith with too much, holding thousands of voices in one view without flattening them into a slogan.

The fair case for the alternatives

The linear ladder

Communicates intent, disciplines planning, funders ask for one. But it assumes value sits only at the top, and has nowhere for the sideways and circular.

Close qualitative reading

The gold standard for depth. But it does not scale to thirteen thousand claims, and no reader can check which quotes a hand summary rests on.

“Too complex to evaluate”

A fair worry that deserves respect. The answer is modesty about the claim.

Causal mapping does not measure how much difference the programme made. It organises the evidence so a human evaluator can see the pathways and weigh them. A smaller claim, and a more defensible one.

What the maps showed

Part two

What the maps showed

What we delivered

Maps at three scales

  • one per country, ten in all
  • one per region
  • one global map

So a finding could be stated nationally, regionally or programme-wide.

Cut thematically too

Capacity strengthening, movement building, advocacy, policy influence, sustainability, each feeding the matching chapter.

Every map came with a written commentary tracing its strongest pathways, counting the links, and saying plainly where the evidence was solid and where it was thin.

What people actually said

An overall map built from the country data. Box size and the numbers show how often a factor was mentioned; arrowhead colour shows positive or negative influence. The largest factor, Love Alliance support for advocacy and capacity building, was the most-cited and the dominant driver.

A story no ladder predicted

Support flows into local partners, which build the capacity of the communities they serve; that capacity feeds advocacy, peer support and a stronger movement.

The story practitioners told was rarely “we delivered outputs and outcomes followed”. It ran closer to:

“We built each other up, and that was the point.”

777

citations for the single most-cited factor, the backbone of that story

Loops a ladder cannot draw

The movement-building view. Networking is the hub, with reinforcing circles: community capacity feeds peer support which feeds capacity again; networking enables advocacy which generates more networking.

Testing the map

Part three

Testing the map, source by source

Read a map source by source

A map of thirteen thousand links is only the beginning. The real work is interrogating it.

For any pathway you can write a vignette, a short commentary from the perspective of the individual sources behind it, and trace each step back to the verbatim quotes that evidence it.

This is where a map is tested and enriched rather than just admired. Each link is a live bookmark: anyone who doubts it can click through to the quote.

Put a doubt to the data

A fair worry surfaced: was the advocacy itself provoking a backlash against key populations?

Rather than argue from impression, we traced the question through the 43 relevant sources. Every account pointed the other way: the support helped communities resist backlash; none named it as the cause.

“also helping to counter the backlash against women’s rights and LGBT rights”

The method holds the positive pathways and the real risks in the same evidence base. Filtering for negative links surfaced a self-reinforcing hostile environment, cited 232 times, which the report drew as the primary threat to sustainability.

Limits, and what comes next

Part four

Limits, and what comes next

What causal mapping does not do

Stating the limits is part of the method.

Filtered

Maps show only the most-mentioned factors. A missing link is not proof the influence is absent, only that it was not among the most cited.

Counts are not strength

A pathway cited a hundred times is not twice as powerful as one cited fifty. And longer chains are always less cited, so downstream outcomes rest on thinner evidence.

Not causal inference

The map does not turn “twenty people said so” into “therefore it is so”. The warranting stays the evaluator’s job.

Why this helps, and what is next

You hold thousands of voices in one picture, at a scale no hand-coding could reach, and still keep faith with each one, because every link carries its quote.

Here the maps tested the programme’s theory of change against the pathways people described, named the main threat to sustainability, and settled the backlash question by going back to the sources. That is evaluative work, done in the open.

So we are ready to carry more of the analysis, working alongside evaluators rather than standing in for their judgement. Read the full case study. App: app.causalmap.app
